content: Appendicitis is the leading cause of acute abdominal pain that necessitates surgical intervention. The exact cause of appendicitis remains uncertain, and its pathogenesis is still a topic of debate. Despite advancements in aseptic techniques and surgical methods, postoperative complications, such as wound infections and intra-abdominal abscesses, continue to contribute significantly to patient morbidity. Several studies suggest that the use of antimicrobial regimens can reduce the incidence of postoperative infections. This review aimed to assess whether the administration of antibiotics, compared to placebo or no treatment, provides benefits to patients undergoing appendectomy. The outcomes were analyzed based on the type of appendicitis, categorized as either simple appendicitis (including non-infectious stages) or complicated appendicitis. However, the review did not evaluate the efficacy of different antibiotic regimens. The search strategy included a comprehensive review of multiple databases, such as The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (Cochrane Library 2005, Issue 1), PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Colorectal Cancer Group Specialised Register (as of April 2005). Additionally, reference lists of the initially identified trials were manually searched for relevant studies. The inclusion criteria focused on Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) and Controlled Clinical Trials (CCTs) that compared any antibiotic regimen to placebo in patients suspected of having appendicitis and undergoing appendectomy. Both pediatric and adult populations were included. The primary outcomes assessed were wound infection, intra-abdominal abscess, length of hospital stay, and mortality. Two reviewers independently assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials, with cross-checking to ensure accuracy. A total of 45 studies, involving 9576 patients, were included in the review. The findings demonstrated that the use of antibiotics was superior to placebo in preventing wound infections and intra-abdominal abscesses. There was no significant difference in outcomes based on the nature of the removed appendix. Studies focusing exclusively on children and those examining the topical application of antibiotics also showed favorable results, although these findings were not statistically significant. The authors concluded that antibiotic prophylaxis is effective in reducing postoperative complications in patients undergoing appendectomy. This benefit was observed regardless of whether the antibiotics were administered preoperatively, perioperatively, or postoperatively. Therefore, the routine use of antibiotic prophylaxis should be considered in emergency appendectomy cases.
